title: Assignment 2
text:
For the trends, particularly the election related keywords it is understandable those most related to the current political news would be appear more in the news. As such it is understanable that Trump would be the highest as he appears more in the news, than election as the midterms are approaching. This also has some correlation with Talarico as he is running in the midterms and made the news recently, the related seach terms like “talarico kimmel” show this. Lastly would be Harris as she has not been in the news for anything important in quite some time. Given this data was gather for the last week, it is split by the hour which aside from a jump on Sept. 12th means the data is just reflecting the daily cycle of the US.This was run again, but using keywords related to the company Flock Safety and for the last month. Overall, these approaches will get the same data but in terms of the main data questions they are not equal. The questions: Reproducibility — could someone else regenerate your file exactly? Provenance — which method records the query parameters for you? Scale — what happens when you need fifty terms instead of three? Fragility — what breaks, and how would you know? The difference can be found even to the first question, as the data pulled down from the website if the parameters are not match perfectly and time stamps are done correctly the data cannot be reproduced. Additionally, it is usually a poor idea to let humans do the data entry for applications like this. To continue in this vein, the provenance is this exact issue. To do the reproduction on from the website one must enter again the parameters from the notes but if done by code it will be recorded in the function call. Example: Keywords: “Trump”,“Harris”,“election”, “Talarico” 9/14 4:20pm US All Cat. Last Week News This will continue in a different way for the scalability, while the code can be set up to take however many strings as you would like the website will take a significantly larger number of button presses for the same result with the addition of greater error risk. To a level further most websites are constructed to not take kindly to bots looking for data particularly when that information could be found with more efficiency from an API call. Lastly, fragility. Websites will always be more fragile than code, that additional level of abstraction for the user experience can introduce more chances for errors and if a website crashes that cause issues with data checks and timing. Code will always have its own unique issues, but generally developers are incentivized to write informative error messages. These differences aside, this does also come down to the nature of the project as for some it would be perfectly reasonable to use a website UI and taking the proper notes rather than going through the trouble of setting up a script which may only get run once.

plot(gtrends(c("Flock Camera","Flock", "automatic license plate reader"), 
                              onlyInterest = TRUE, 
                              geo = "US", time = "today 1-m"))







# 1. Read the dataset and trim any column whitespace
df <- read.csv("gtrend_flock.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(df) <- trimws(names(df))

# 2. Convert Time to Date class
df$Time <- as.Date(df$Time, format = "%Y-%m-%d")

# 3. Identify series and assign distinct line colors
terms <- names(df)[-1]
line_colors <- c("#1F77B4", "#FF7F0E", "#2CA02C")

# 4. Configure margins to accommodate rotated date labels
par(mar = c(6, 4.5, 3.5, 2))

# 5. Initialize the plot canvas with a daily custom x-axis
plot(
  df$Time, df[[terms[1]]],
  type = "n",
  ylim = c(0, max(df[, terms], na.rm = TRUE) * 1.05),
  xaxt = "n",
  xlab = "",
  ylab = "Relative Search Interest (0–100)",
  main = "Daily Google Trends Interest Over Time",
  las = 1
)
title(xlab = "Date", line = 4.5)

# 6. Add light gridlines
grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "gray85", lty = 1)

# 7. Draw daily axis ticks rotated vertically
daily_ticks <- seq(from = min(df$Time), to = max(df$Time), by = "1 day")
axis.Date(
  side = 1,
  at = daily_ticks,
  format = "%b %d",
  las = 2,
  cex.axis = 0.7
)

# 8. Draw lines for each term
for (i in seq_along(terms)) {
  lines(df$Time, df[[terms[i]]], col = line_colors[i], lwd = 2, type = "o", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
}

# 9. Add legend
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = terms,
  col = line_colors,
  lwd = 2,
  pch = 16,
  bty = "n",
  cex = 0.85
)

title: Assignment 3
text:
The goal of this was to examine rural urban splits at the county level. Geography: County (State: California) Variables:

Renter occupied housing units
Number of households
Number of enrolled students

A rent rate is calculated as the percentage of households renting. (renter occupied) / (total households) Assumptions: Large percent of renters and a larger number of students in urban counties, showing a younger and more transient population. The margin of error show the uncertainty around the values being mapped. This and the related uncertainty intervals can show if counties are statically different in their rent rates (or not significant if there is an overlap) Interpretation: The map demonstrates the number of students is higher in those urban counties, this is more a reflection of the population density but can also be viewed as the population is younger. Most of the top 10 in rent percent also are major urban counties. (Namely, San Francisco County & Los Angeles)

—- 5. The question this script exists to raise ————————— Compare 2 and 3. Same concept, two data-generating processes: - Wikipedia: edited by volunteers, sourced from many places, no schema, no versioning, no uncertainty, changes without notice - World Bank: one compiler, documented methodology, stable indicator code Scraping was the wrong tool here. Knowing when it is the only tool is the skill this course is actually teaching.
The time stamps on the World Bank data is probably the most imporant part of understanding the scraping, this gives a point of reference to check the data against. While Wikipedia is a decent source, to get those same timestamp if would likely require scraping (or using the api) of each bank being referenced in the table. As is stated, scraping is best when it is the only tool available. APIs or other data access points get around all of those messy data issues which come from even the most successful scraping attempts.
AI note Gemini was used for dealing with the tibble and visualizations.

—- 5. The question this script exists to raise ————————— Compare 2 and 3. Same concept, two data-generating processes: - Wikipedia: edited by volunteers, sourced from many places, no schema, no versioning, no uncertainty, changes without notice - World Bank: one compiler, documented methodology, stable indicator code Scraping was the wrong tool here. Knowing when it is the only tool is the skill this course is actually teaching.
The time stamps on the World Bank data is probably the most imporant part of understanding the scraping, this gives a point of reference to check the data against. While Wikipedia is a decent source, to get those same timestamp if would likely require scraping (or using the api) of each bank being referenced in the table. As is stated, scraping is best when it is the only tool available. APIs or other data access points get around all of those messy data issues which come from even the most successful scraping attempts.
AI note Gemini was used for dealing with the tibble and visualizations.

  tibble(

    rating = pods |> html_element(".star-rating") |> html_attr("class"),
    stock = pods |> html_element(".availability") |> html_text2()

}

The manual download and the API query get different results, likely due to different keywords being entered in the website.

Report
Gov Info provide very good information, being that they are digital documents and not photo scans or otherwise physical to digital documents. It would take a little work through quanteda or some other semantic tool to process all the documents. A good way to improve the process in question could be in processing a combination of the title and governmentAuthor to better specify what documents are being searched for. This could also be done with the small description included with the document that as well, but would need more implementation of a semantic search tool.
The advantage of an API over a search page or scraping is the level of control if offers. The data searched by the API will be structured and sorted intentionally for quick, accurate, and repeatable access.

text:
###Tweets: ##Background: This summit was a notable meeting between the Chinese and US leaders to try and defuse some of the tensions which had been building during that time. It resulted in generally a favorable aspect between the two leaders. In the comparisons of the tweets which came out about that time, it is not overly surprising that the Xi administration linked to terms related to China more and the US administration linked to terms related to the US. The interesting part comes from the comparison of the use terms which came out of the summit, even as the tweets tend to be a rather limited view of the situation and biased to a given topic as the tweets gathered were all in English. From the documents it can be seen that both sides were using generally positive terms in regards to the situation, like relationship compromise and deepening. However, amusingly China referred to itself more than anything other while the US had nations as their most used term.
###Quantitative Text Analysis In the comparison of the presidential inaugural addresses, this is being done on length, word diversity, and readability. Additionally, these addresses can be understood on the cosine similarity and keyness by party. In terms of length, which can be can be understood in the number of tokens needed to process the address. However, despite the want of politicians to talk the number of tokens has not changed overly much across all the addresses. The one which has changed greatly is that of the word choice and complexity. As the decades have moved, and the understanding of who the address is aimed at has changed there is a notable drop in the complexity of the language being used measured in US grade level. Even despite this, there are still a lot of consistent words which will continue to be used between addresses and even addresses of a similar era will remain generally consistent. For example, topics like jobs or drugs will be usually relegated to more modern speakers, but terms like government or people are very often present with good reason. These are notable and well crafted address which are meant to be a summation of nation concerns and the beginning of some era of change, but these sorts of consistencies between addresses point to an amusing level of irony behind that particular concept.

api_key <- Sys.getenv("GOVINFO_API_KEY")
if (api_key == "") {
  warning("GOVINFO_API_KEY environment variable not set. Falling back to DEMO_KEY (subject to strict rate limits).")
  api_key <- "DEMO_KEY"
}
save_dir <- "govInfo_CPD_Xi"
if (!dir.exists(save_dir)) {
  dir.create(save_dir, recursive = TRUE)
}

search_query <- 'collection:(CPD) AND "Xi Jinping" AND publishdate:range(2021-01-20,)'
all_records <- list()
offset_mark <- "*"
page_size   <- 100
page_count  <- 1
total_count <- NA

repeat {
  message(sprintf("--> Fetching page %d (offsetMark: %s)...", page_count, offset_mark))
  
  req_body <- list(
    query      = search_query,
    pageSize   = page_size,
    offsetMark = offset_mark,
    sorts      = list(list(field = "publishdate", sortOrder = "DESC"))
  )
  
  resp <- tryCatch({
    request("https://api.govinfo.gov/search") |>
      req_url_query(api_key = api_key) |>
      req_body_json(req_body) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()
  }, error = function(e) {
    message("Error during API request: ", conditionMessage(e))
    NULL
  })
  
  if (is.null(resp) || is.null(resp$results) || length(resp$results) == 0) {
    message("No more records returned from API.")
    break
  }
  
  if (is.na(total_count) && !is.null(resp$count)) {
    total_count <- resp$count
    message(sprintf("Total matching CPD documents identified in GovInfo: %d", total_count))
  }
  
  batch <- resp$results
  all_records <- c(all_records, batch)
  message(sprintf("    Retrieved %d records (running total: %d of %s)", 
                  length(batch), length(all_records), ifelse(is.na(total_count), "?", as.character(total_count))))
  next_offset <- resp$offsetMark
  if (is.null(next_offset) || next_offset == offset_mark || 
      (!is.na(total_count) && length(all_records) >= total_count)) {
    message("Reached final page of search results.")
    break
  }
  
  offset_mark <- next_offset
  page_count  <- page_count + 1
  Sys.sleep(0.5) # politeness buffer
}

download_log <- lapply(seq_along(all_records), function(i) {
  item <- all_records[[i]]
  pkg_id <- item$packageId
  
  pdf_url <- if (!is.null(item$download$pdfLink)) {
    item$download$pdfLink
  } else {
    paste0("https://api.govinfo.gov/packages/", pkg_id, "/pdf")
  }
  
  file_name <- paste0(pkg_id, ".pdf")
  dest_path <- file.path(save_dir, file_name)
  if (file.exists(dest_path) && file.size(dest_path) > 0) {
    status <- "Already Downloaded"
  } else {
    status <- tryCatch({
      request(pdf_url) |>
        req_url_query(api_key = api_key) |>
        req_perform(path = dest_path)
      "Success"
    }, error = function(e) {
      conditionMessage(e)
    })
    Sys.sleep(0.2)
  }
  
  data.frame(
    index        = i,
    package_id   = pkg_id,
    date_issued  = if (!is.null(item$dateIssued)) item$dateIssued else NA_character_,
    title        = if (!is.null(item$title)) item$title else NA_character_,
    collection   = if (!is.null(item$collectionCode)) item$collectionCode else "CPD",
    pdf_url      = pdf_url,
    file_path    = dest_path,
    size_mb      = if (file.exists(dest_path)) round(file.size(dest_path) / (1024^2), 2) else NA_real_,
    status       = status,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})

biden_regex <- "\\b(biden|joe|potus|whitehouse|washington|us|u\\.s|usa|america|american)\\b"
xi_regex    <- "\\b(xi|jinping|china|chinese|beijing|ccp|prc)\\b"

raw_texts <- tolower(as.character(tweet_corpus))
has_biden <- str_detect(raw_texts, biden_regex)
has_xi    <- str_detect(raw_texts, xi_regex)

docvars(tweet_corpus, "admin_focus") <- case_when(
  has_biden & !has_xi ~ "Biden_Admin",
  !has_biden & has_xi ~ "Xi_Admin",
  has_biden & has_xi  ~ "Bilateral",
  TRUE                ~ "Other"
)

title: Assignment 7
text:
A YouTube comment section under 2026 U.S. midterm election coverage is neither a probability sample of the American electorate nor a representative mirror of a news channel’s viewership. Instead, it is the product of a multi-stage data-generating process shaped by platform ranking algorithms, broadcaster editorial choices, audience self-selection, and automated moderation (Freelon 2018; YouTube Data API v3 Documentation). Understanding what our quanteda keyness and sentiment models actually measure requires tracing each filter between a political event and the rows returned by tuber.
First, video discovery itself is a ranking rather than a census. Querying "US midterm election" via yt_search() for the pre-election window (1 September – 27 October 2026) and post-election window (from 4 November 2026 onward) under order = "relevance" versus order = "viewCount" yields markedly different candidate pools, even while attr(x, "total_results") reports a vastly larger universe than the 100 items returned per two-page search call. Because search.list costs 100 quota units and 1 search call per page, retrieving channel uploads directly via list_channel_videos() (playlistItems.list, costing 1 unit per 50 videos) across three distinct broadcaster types—NBC News (national broadcast network, UCeY0bbntWzzVIaj2z3QigXg), Fox News (cable news network, UCXIJgqnII2ZOINSWNOGFThA), and BBC News (international public broadcaster, UC16niRr50-MSBwiO3YDb3RA)—surfaces campaign coverage that generic keyword search misses, while exposing the trade-off of regex title filtering ("midterm|election|senate|house race|ballot"), which captures explicit horse-race headlines but drops candidate-named segments and occasionally admits non-U.S. ballot stories on international feeds.
Second, within selected videos, the gap between the comment_count reported by get_video_stats() and the comments retrieved by collect_comments() (n_max = 300) reflects four structural truncations: (1) our 300-comment collection cap, which samples the earliest or top-ranked thread pages; (2) comments held for creator review or removed by YouTube’s spam filters; (3) channel-level policy decisions to disable comment sections entirely on sensitive political broadcasts (recorded as status = "disabled" in our collection log); and (4) nested reply cascades (is_reply = TRUE). Engagement and authorship within open comment sections are heavily skewed: the top 1% of comments capture a disproportionate share of all like_count endorsements, while the top 10% most active commenters and repeated slogan or copy-pasted strings account for a substantial fraction of total volume. Consequently, unadjusted bag-of-words counts overweight vocal repeat participants.
Third, reading keywords in context (kwic()) for democrat*, republican*, trump, vote*, and ballot* prior to modeling shows that commenter invocations overwhelmingly express partisan grievances or candidate evaluations rather than neutral procedural descriptions. When we compound multi-word political phrases (house majority, senate race, early voting, mail in, election fraud, red wave, and voter id) and estimate differential keyness (textstat_keyness()), channel contrasts reflect the distinct audiences attracted to NBC News, Fox News, and BBC News rather than intrinsic differences in the election itself. Meanwhile, comparing pre-election against post-election comments captures the shift from mobilization and procedural suspicion (early voting, mail in, ballot) to outcome attribution (house majority, senate race). Validating the Lexicoder Sentiment Dictionary (data_dictionary_LSD2015) against 40 hand-coded comments further demonstrates why off-the-shelf dictionaries misread campaign discourse: competitive metaphors ("landslide", "beat", "fight"), fraud allegations ("rigged"), and pervasive sarcasm cause lexical lookup to conflate conflict framing with negative affect and ironic praise with positive sentiment.
Finally, comparing this YouTube collection against our two corpora from Assignment 6 clarifies what claims each source can support:



Dimension
2021 Biden–Xi Summit Tweets (Assignment 6)
GovInfo Presidential Documents (CPD) Mentioning Xi (Assignment 6)
2026 US Midterm YouTube Comments (Assignment 7)




Who Produced the Text
Politicians, media outlets (e.g., NYT journalists), activists, and English-language Twitter users (\(N = 4,903\) deduplicated tweets).
The U.S. President and White House Press Office (\(N = 351\) official CPD packages from 20 Jan 2021 forward; plus 60 historical Inaugural Addresses).
Pseudonymous YouTube viewers and repeat commenters reacting under NBC News, Fox News, and BBC News videos.


For Whom (Intended Audience)
Public platform followers, journalists, and transnational digital publics monitoring the virtual summit.
Domestic citizens, Congress, foreign governments (Beijing), and the permanent statutory record.
Fellow channel viewers, content creators, and partisan communities in the comment thread.


What Selected It
Keyword/hashtag capture around the Nov 2021 summit, filtered to distinct English-language (lang == "en") posts.
Statutory publication in the Compilation of Presidential Documents retrieved via GovInfo Search API (collection:(CPD) AND "Xi Jinping").
YouTube ranking (relevance/viewCount), channel upload lists, regex title filter, channel moderation, and a 300-comment/video cap.


Can It Be Collected Again?
No (Restricted): Pre-compiled CSV remains accessible, but live Twitter/X API re-collection is blocked by post-API paywalls (Freelon 2018).
Yes (Permanent): Public-domain government records on GovInfo can be re-queried and re-downloaded indefinitely with an API key.
Partially (Ephemeral): Raw comments are non-authorized API data that must be deleted within 30 days (Policy III.E.4.d); re-running the manifest yields shifted rankings and deleted comments.


Claim It Can Support
Claims about platform-mediated framing during a diplomatic event (e.g., Biden_Admin \(n=82\) emphasizing nations [\(\chi^2=49.17\)] and guardrails [\(\chi^2=30.02\)] vs. Xi_Admin \(n=133\) emphasizing china [\(\chi^2=-43.91\)] and compromise [\(\chi^2=-9.23\)]).
Claims about official government statecraft and institutional rhetoric (e.g., diplomatic framing of Xi Jinping or inaugural readability declining from Grade 23.1 to Grade 9.3).
Claims about the comments YouTube showed an audience on specific news channels before and after Election Day—not claims about voters at large.



In short, whereas Assignment 6’s GovInfo CPD collection supports institutional claims about a government and the 2021 summit tweets capture platform discourse around a bilateral summit, our 2026 YouTube corpus describes the moderated comments YouTube surfaced under specific media channels’ audiences.

title: Assignment 7
text:
Data Note: YouTube 2026 Midterm Collection

Source: YouTube Data API v3 accessed via the development version of the R package tuber (>= 2.0.0.9000) and httr2 (>= 1.1.0).
Permission & Compliance: Collected using a personal Google Cloud API key (YOUTUBE_KEY stored in .Renviron, excluded via .gitignore) querying public read endpoints only (skipping OAuth). Per the YouTube API Services Developer Policies (Sections III.E.4.d and III.E.6), comments retrieved via an API key constitute non-authorized data subject to a strict 30-day retention limit (delete_by recorded in manifest_pre.json and manifest_post.json), after which data/youtube/ must be deleted. No external page or transcript scrapers (yt-dlp) were used, and all commenter usernames (author_name) and channel IDs (author_channel_id) are excluded from published outputs.
Quota Budget: Managed under YouTube’s dual daily budgets of 10,000 quota units/day and 100 search calls/day (YouTube Quota Calculator), planned prior to execution and reconciled via yt_get_quota_usage().
Method:

Search Route: Queried term = "US midterm election" (max_results = 100, 2 pages per query) twice per period using order = "relevance" and order = "viewCount" across two windows: Pre-Election (2026-09-01T00:00:00Z to 2026-10-28T00:00:00Z) and Post-Election (2026-11-04T00:00:00Z to collection date).
Channel Route: Queried get_channel_details() and list_channel_videos() (playlistItems.list, 1 unit per 50 uploads) for three channels differing in kind: NBC News (UCeY0bbntWzzVIaj2z3QigXg, national broadcast network), Fox News (UCXIJgqnII2ZOINSWNOGFThA, cable news channel), and BBC News (UC16niRr50-MSBwiO3YDb3RA, international broadcaster), filtering titles with the case-insensitive regex "midterm|election|senate|house race|ballot".
Comment Collection: Up to 4 election videos per channel per period, capped at n_max = 300 comments (including replies) per video via collect_comments() wrapping get_all_comments().

Selection & Deduplication: Search results were deduplicated on video_id (distinct(video_id, .keep_all = TRUE)) prior to joining get_video_stats(), and comments were deduplicated on comment_id (distinct(comment_id, .keep_all = TRUE)) before many-to-one metadata joins (relationship = "many-to-one").
Known Gaps: (1) High-volume news channels upload 30–50+ clips daily, requiring 30–60+ paginated playlistItems calls (1,500–3,000+ videos) to reach 1 September 2026; (2) title regex filtering omits videos that reference only candidate surnames without explicit election keywords; (3) channels that disable comments (status = "disabled"), moderator-deleted/held comments, and threads exceeding the 300-comment cap are unobserved; and (4) YouTube rounds public subscriber_count values.

# Part 5c: Polite comment collection helper recording ok, disabled, none, or error
collect_comments <- function(video_id, n_max = 300) {
  status <- "ok"
  out <- tryCatch(
    withCallingHandlers(
      get_all_comments(video_id, max_results = n_max),
      tuber_comments_disabled = function(w) {
        status <<- "disabled"
        invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
      },
      tuber_no_comments = function(w) {
        if (status == "ok") status <<- "none"
        invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
      }
    ),
    error = function(e) e
  )
  Sys.sleep(1)
  if (inherits(out, "error")) {
    return(list(
      data = NULL,
      log  = tibble(
        video_id = video_id,
        status   = "error",
        n        = 0L,
        message  = conditionMessage(out)
      )
    ))
  }
  df_out <- as_tibble(out)
  list(
    data = df_out,
    log  = tibble(
      video_id = video_id,
      status   = status,
      n        = nrow(df_out),
      message  = NA_character_
    )
  )
}

3b. Read, Then Count (quanteda)

3b.i. Corpus Construction and Preprocessing Choices
We construct the quanteda corpus at the individual comment level (docid_field = "comment_id"), preserving is_reply as a document variable so top-level statements and reply interactions can be analyzed together or stratified. Before tokenizing, we strip @username mentions (@[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+) to prevent commenter handles from leaking into feature tables, remove URLs (remove_url = TRUE), and remove punctuation and Unicode emoji/symbol characters (remove_punct = TRUE, remove_symbols = TRUE) so keyness and sentiment models reflect lexical content rather than graphical reaction symbols.

# 3b.i: Build corpus with required docvars and clean @mentions, URLs, and symbols/emoji
corp_yt <- comments_metrics |>
  mutate(
    date       = as.Date(published_at),
    text_clean = str_replace_all(text_original, "@[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+", " ")
  ) |>
  select(
    comment_id,
    text_clean,
    channel_title,
    video_id,
    is_reply,
    like_count,
    date,
    period
  ) |>
  corpus(docid_field = "comment_id", text_field = "text_clean")

# Summarize corpus at aggregate level (without printing raw comment IDs/authors)
tibble(
  Total_Documents = ndoc(corp_yt),
  Channels = paste(unique(docvars(corp_yt, "channel_title")), collapse = ", "),
  Periods = paste(unique(docvars(corp_yt, "period")), collapse = ", "),
  Date_Min = as.character(min(docvars(corp_yt, "date"), na.rm = TRUE)),
  Date_Max = as.character(max(docvars(corp_yt, "date"), na.rm = TRUE))
) |> kable(caption = "Part 3b.i: YouTube Comment Corpus Overview")

3b.ii. Keywords in Context (kwic()) Reading & Functional Tally
We run kwic() across the five required patterns (democrat*, republican*, trump, vote*, ballot*), inspect up to 20 concordance lines per pattern, and tally whether each occurrence is primarily naming a party, naming a candidate, describing the voting process, or expressing a grievance/fraud allegation (per Part 4b, we report the aggregate functional classification rather than dumping raw unredacted comment strings).

toks_raw <- tokens(
  corp_yt,
  remove_punct   = TRUE,
  remove_url     = TRUE,
  remove_symbols = TRUE
) |>
  tokens_tolower()

kwic_patterns <- c("democrat*", "republican*", "trump", "vote*", "ballot*")

kwic_20_each <- map_dfr(kwic_patterns, function(pat) {
  kw <- kwic(toks_raw, pattern = pat, window = 6)
  as_tibble(kw) |>
    mutate(target_pattern = pat) |>
    slice_head(n = 20)
})

# Classify what each KWIC line is doing based on context window (pre + keyword + post)
kwic_classified <- kwic_20_each |>
  mutate(
    context_window = paste(pre, keyword, post),
    function_category = case_when(
      str_detect(context_window, "fraud|rigged|cheat|steal|stolen|fake|corrupt|lie|lies|shame|destroy|blame") ~ "Grievance / Fraud Claim",
      str_detect(target_pattern, "trump") | str_detect(context_window, "trump|biden|harris|vance|candidate|nominee") ~ "Naming a Candidate",
      str_detect(target_pattern, "vote\\*|ballot\\*") &
        str_detect(context_window, "mail|early|count|box|poll|register|id|day|cast|turnout|machine") ~ "Voting Process / Logistics",
      str_detect(target_pattern, "democrat\\*|republican\\*") |
        str_detect(context_window, "party|dems|gop|left|right|liberal|conservative|majority|senate|house") ~ "Naming a Party / Coalition",
      TRUE ~ "Voting Process / General Evaluation"
    )
  )

kwic_tally <- kwic_classified |>
  count(target_pattern, function_category) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = function_category, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(Lines_Inspected = rowSums(across(where(is.numeric))))

set.seed(42)

# Create Texas Government Employee Data (TRS - Teacher Retirement System)
create_trs_data <- function(n = 500) {
  
  first_names <- c("John", "Maria", "Robert", "Jennifer", "Michael", "Sarah",
                   "David", "Patricia", "James", "Linda", "Daniel", "Barbara")
  last_names <- c("Smith", "Johnson", "Williams", "Brown", "Jones", "Garcia",
                  "Miller", "Davis", "Rodriguez", "Martinez", "Hernandez", "Lopez")
  
  trs <- tibble(
    record_id = paste0("TRS_", 1:n),
    first_name = sample(first_names, n, replace = TRUE),
    last_name = sample(last_names, n, replace = TRUE),
    dob = sample(seq(as.Date("1950-01-01"), as.Date("1985-12-31"), by = "day"), n),
    years_service = sample(5:40, n, replace = TRUE),
    salary_group = sample(c("Elementary", "Secondary", "Administration"), n, replace = TRUE),
    retirement_date = NA_Date_
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      # Some retirements for older employees
      retirement_date = case_when(
        years_service > 30 ~ as.Date(paste0(2020 + sample(0:4, n, replace = TRUE), 
                                              "-", 
                                              sample(1:12, n, replace = TRUE, prob = rep(1/12, 12)),
                                              "-01")),
        TRUE ~ NA_Date_
      )
    )
  
  return(trs)
}

# Create Education Agency Data (TEA - Texas Education Agency)
create_tea_data <- function(trs, n = 500, num_matches = 100, corruption_rate = 0.2) {
  
  first_names <- c("John", "Maria", "Robert", "Jennifer", "Michael", "Sarah",
                   "David", "Patricia", "James", "Linda", "Daniel", "Barbara",
                   "Jon", "Mary", "Rob", "Jen", "Mike", "Sara")  # Include variations
  last_names <- c("Smith", "Smithe", "Smyth", "Johnson", "Jonson", "Williams", 
                  "Brown", "Jones", "Garcia", "Miller", "Davis", "Rodriguez", 
                  "Martinez", "Hernandez", "Lopez", "Sanchez")
  
  tea <- tibble(
    record_id = paste0("TEA_", 1:n),
    first_name = sample(first_names, n, replace = TRUE),
    last_name = sample(last_names, n, replace = TRUE),
    dob = sample(seq(as.Date("1950-01-01"), as.Date("1985-12-31"), by = "day"), n),
    certification = sample(c("Science", "Math", "English", "Social Studies", "Special Ed"), n, replace = TRUE),
    school_district = sample(paste0("District_", 1:50), n, replace = TRUE),
    hire_date = sample(seq(as.Date("1990-01-01"), as.Date("2020-12-31"), by = "day"), n)
  )
  
  # Make the first num_matches TEA records true matches of TRS_1..TRS_num_matches.
  # The remaining TEA records are unrelated people (true non-matches).
  tea$first_name[1:num_matches] <- trs$first_name[1:num_matches]
  tea$last_name[1:num_matches] <- trs$last_name[1:num_matches]
  tea$dob[1:num_matches] <- trs$dob[1:num_matches]

  # Introduce data quality issues in the matched records only
  # About 20% of matched records have corruption or variation
  corruption_indices <- sample(1:num_matches, size = round(num_matches * corruption_rate), replace = FALSE)
  
  for (idx in corruption_indices) {
    flip <- sample(1:3, 1)
    
    if (flip == 1) {
      # Introduce name variation
      tea$first_name[idx] <- abbreviate(tea$first_name[idx], minlength = 3)
    } else if (flip == 2) {
      # Introduce small typo in last name
      last_chars <- nchar(tea$last_name[idx])
      if (last_chars > 1) {
        typo_pos <- sample(1:last_chars, 1)
        wrong_char <- sample(letters[!(letters %in% unlist(strsplit(tea$last_name[idx], "")))], 1)
        tea$last_name[idx] <- paste0(
          substr(tea$last_name[idx], 1, typo_pos - 1),
          wrong_char,
          substr(tea$last_name[idx], typo_pos + 1, last_chars)
        )
      }
    } else {
      # Shift DOB slightly (data entry error)
      tea$dob[idx] <- tea$dob[idx] + sample(c(-1, 1), 1)
    }
  }
  
  return(tea)
}

# Create a subset of KNOWN matches for validation
create_validation_set <- function(trs, tea, num_matches = 100) {
  
  # Take first 100 records from TRS
  trs_subset <- trs %>% slice(1:num_matches)
  
  # These are the "true" matches in TEA
  true_matches <- tea %>%
    slice(1:num_matches) %>%
    rename_with(~paste0("tea_", .), everything()) %>%
    rename(tea_record_id = tea_record_id)
  
  # Create ground truth
  validation <- tibble(
    trs_record_id = trs_subset$record_id,
    tea_record_id = true_matches$tea_record_id,
    is_match = TRUE
  )
  
  return(validation)
}

# ============================================================================
# PART 3: DETERMINISTIC LINKAGE RULES
# ============================================================================

deterministic_linkage <- function(data_a, data_b, 
                                  id_col_a = "record_id", 
                                  id_col_b = "record_id") {
  
  log_info("Starting deterministic linkage...")
  
  matches <- tibble()
  remaining_a <- data_a
  remaining_b <- data_b
  
  # RULE 1: Exact match on last name + first name + DOB
  # (Highest confidence)
  log_info("Applying Rule 1: Last name + First name + DOB")
  
  rule1 <- remaining_a %>%
    inner_join(
      remaining_b,
      by = c("last_name_std" = "last_name_std",
             "first_name_std" = "first_name_std",
             "dob_std" = "dob_std"),
      suffix = c("_a", "_b")
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      rule_applied = "Rule_1_FullName_DOB",
      confidence = 0.99
    ) %>%
    select(!!sym(paste0(id_col_a, "_a")), 
           !!sym(paste0(id_col_b, "_b")), 
           rule_applied, confidence)
  
  matches <- bind_rows(matches, rule1)
  
  # Remove matched records
  remaining_a <- anti_join(remaining_a, rule1, by = setNames("record_id_a", id_col_a))
  remaining_b <- anti_join(remaining_b, rule1, by = setNames("record_id_b", id_col_b))
  
  log_info(paste("Rule 1 found", nrow(rule1), "matches"))
  
  # RULE 2: Last name + First initial + DOB
  # (For records where first name varies slightly)
  log_info("Applying Rule 2: Last name + First initial + DOB")
  
  rule2 <- remaining_a %>%
    inner_join(
      remaining_b,
      by = c("last_name_std" = "last_name_std",
             "first_initial" = "first_initial",
             "dob_std" = "dob_std"),
      suffix = c("_a", "_b")
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      rule_applied = "Rule_2_LastName_Initial_DOB",
      confidence = 0.95
    ) %>%
    select(record_id_a, record_id_b, rule_applied, confidence)

  matches <- bind_rows(matches, rule2)
  remaining_a <- anti_join(remaining_a, rule2, by = setNames("record_id_a", id_col_a))
  remaining_b <- anti_join(remaining_b, rule2, by = setNames("record_id_b", id_col_b))
  
  log_info(paste("Rule 2 found", nrow(rule2), "matches"))
  
  # RULE 3: Last name + First name + DOB within 1 day
  # (For data entry errors on DOB)
  log_info("Applying Rule 3: Last name + First name + DOB (±1 day)")
  
  rule3 <- remaining_a %>%
    cross_join(remaining_b, suffix = c("_a", "_b")) %>%
    filter(
      last_name_std_a == last_name_std_b,
      first_name_std_a == first_name_std_b,
      abs(as.numeric(difftime(dob_std_a, dob_std_b, units = "days"))) <= 1
    ) %>%
    select(record_id_a, record_id_b) %>%
    mutate(
      rule_applied = "Rule_3_DOBFlex",
      confidence = 0.90
    )

  if (nrow(rule3) > 0) {
    # Remove duplicates (keep first match only)
    rule3 <- rule3 %>% distinct(record_id_a, .keep_all = TRUE)
    matches <- bind_rows(matches, rule3)
    remaining_a <- anti_join(remaining_a, rule3, by = setNames("record_id_a", id_col_a))
    remaining_b <- anti_join(remaining_b, rule3, by = setNames("record_id_b", id_col_b))
  }
  
  log_info(paste("Rule 3 found", nrow(rule3), "matches"))
  
  result <- list(
    matches = matches,
    remaining_a = remaining_a,
    remaining_b = remaining_b,
    summary = tibble(
      Rule = c("Rule 1", "Rule 2", "Rule 3"),
      Matches = c(nrow(rule1), nrow(rule2), nrow(rule3))
    )
  )
  
  return(result)
}

# Calculate string similarity using Jaro-Winkler
calculate_string_similarity <- function(str1, str2, method = "jw") {
  
  if (is.na(str1) | is.na(str2)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  
  # Jaro-Winkler returns distance (0-1), we want similarity
  1 - stringdist(str1, str2, method = method)
}

# More efficient: Use vectorized stringdistmatrix
calculate_similarity_efficient <- function(data_a_field, data_b_field) {
  
  dist_matrix <- stringdistmatrix(
    data_a_field,
    data_b_field,
    method = "jw",
    useNames = "strings"
  )
  
  # Convert distance to similarity (1 - distance)
  similarity <- 1 - dist_matrix
  
  return(similarity)
}

# ============================================================================
# ASSESSMENT: PRECISION, RECALL, F1-SCORE
# ============================================================================

assess_linkage_quality <- function(all_matches, validation_set) {
  
  log_info("Assessing linkage quality against validation set...")
  
  our_matches <- all_matches %>%
    mutate(our_match = 1) %>%
    select(trs_record_id, tea_record_id, our_match)
  
  true_matches <- validation_set %>%
    rename(trs_record_id = trs_record_id, 
           tea_record_id = tea_record_id) %>%
    mutate(true_match = 1) %>%
    select(trs_record_id, tea_record_id, true_match)
  
  # Full outer join to get all possibilities
  assessment <- true_matches %>%
    full_join(our_matches, 
              by = c("trs_record_id", "tea_record_id")) %>%
    mutate(
      true_match = replace_na(true_match, 0),
      our_match = replace_na(our_match, 0)
    )
  
  tp <- sum(assessment$true_match == 1 & assessment$our_match == 1)
  fp <- sum(assessment$true_match == 0 & assessment$our_match == 1)
  fn <- sum(assessment$true_match == 1 & assessment$our_match == 0)
  tn <- sum(assessment$true_match == 0 & assessment$our_match == 0)
  
  precision <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else NA_real_
  recall <- if (tp + fn > 0) tp / (tp + fn) else NA_real_
  f1 <- if (!is.na(precision) & !is.na(recall) & precision + recall > 0) {
    2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall)
  } else {
    NA_real_
  }
  
  accuracy <- (tp + tn) / nrow(assessment)
  
  results <- list(
    metrics = tibble(
      Metric = c("Precision", "Recall", "F1-Score", "Accuracy"),
      Value = c(precision, recall, f1, accuracy),
      Interpretation = c(
        "Of matches we made, what % were correct?",
        "Of all true matches, what % did we find?",
        "Harmonic mean of precision and recall",
        "What % of all decisions were correct?"
      )
    ),
    confusion_matrix = tibble(
      Metric = c("True Positives", "False Positives", "False Negatives", "True Negatives"),
      Count = c(tp, fp, fn, tn)
    ),
    detailed = assessment
  )
  
  return(results)
}

# ============================================================================
# PART 7: SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS
# ============================================================================

sensitivity_analysis <- function(all_comparisons, validation_df = validation_set, include_deterministic = FALSE, det_matches = NULL) {
  
  log_info("Running sensitivity analysis on thresholds...")
  thresholds <- seq(0.70, 0.99, by = 0.05)
  results <- tibble()
  
  for (threshold in thresholds) {
    test_matches <- all_comparisons %>%
      filter(match_score >= threshold) %>%
      mutate(our_match = 1) %>%
      select(record_id_a, record_id_b, our_match)
    
    if (include_deterministic && !is.null(det_matches)) {
      test_matches <- bind_rows(
        det_matches %>% select(record_id_a, record_id_b) %>% mutate(our_match = 1),
        test_matches
      ) %>% distinct(record_id_a, record_id_b, .keep_all = TRUE)
    }
    
    # Full validation
    assessment <- validation_df %>%
      rename(record_id_a = trs_record_id, record_id_b = tea_record_id) %>%
      full_join(test_matches, by = c("record_id_a", "record_id_b")) %>%
      mutate(
        is_match = replace_na(is_match, 0),
        our_match = replace_na(our_match, 0)
      )
    
    tp <- sum(assessment$is_match == 1 & assessment$our_match == 1)
    fp <- sum(assessment$is_match == 0 & assessment$our_match == 1)
    fn <- sum(assessment$is_match == 1 & assessment$our_match == 0)
    
    precision <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else 0
    recall <- if (tp + fn > 0) tp / (tp + fn) else 0
    f1 <- if (precision + recall > 0) 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall) else 0
    
    results <- bind_rows(results, tibble(
      threshold = threshold,
      num_matches = nrow(test_matches),
      precision = precision,
      recall = recall,
      f1 = f1
    ))
  }
  return(results)
}

# Create Texas Government Employee Data (TRS - Teacher Retirement System)
create_trs_data <- function(n = 500) {
  
  first_names <- c("John", "Maria", "Robert", "Jennifer", "Michael", "Sarah",
                   "David", "Patricia", "James", "Linda", "Daniel", "Barbara")
  last_names <- c("Smith", "Johnson", "Williams", "Brown", "Jones", "Garcia",
                  "Miller", "Davis", "Rodriguez", "Martinez", "Hernandez", "Lopez")
  
  trs <- tibble(
    record_id = paste0("TRS_", 1:n),
    first_name = sample(first_names, n, replace = TRUE),
    last_name = sample(last_names, n, replace = TRUE),
    dob = sample(seq(as.Date("1950-01-01"), as.Date("1985-12-31"), by = "day"), n),
    years_service = sample(5:40, n, replace = TRUE),
    salary_group = sample(c("Elementary", "Secondary", "Administration"), n, replace = TRUE),
    retirement_date = NA_Date_
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      # Some retirements for older employees
      retirement_date = case_when(
        years_service > 30 ~ as.Date(paste0(2020 + sample(0:4, n, replace = TRUE), 
                                              "-", 
                                              sample(1:12, n, replace = TRUE, prob = rep(1/12, 12)),
                                              "-01")),
        TRUE ~ NA_Date_
      )
    )
  
  return(trs)
}

# Create Education Agency Data (TEA - Texas Education Agency)
create_tea_data <- function(trs, n = 500, num_matches = 100, corruption_rate = 0.2) {
  
  first_names <- c("John", "Maria", "Robert", "Jennifer", "Michael", "Sarah",
                   "David", "Patricia", "James", "Linda", "Daniel", "Barbara",
                   "Jon", "Mary", "Rob", "Jen", "Mike", "Sara")  # Include variations
  last_names <- c("Smith", "Smithe", "Smyth", "Johnson", "Jonson", "Williams", 
                  "Brown", "Jones", "Garcia", "Miller", "Davis", "Rodriguez", 
                  "Martinez", "Hernandez", "Lopez", "Sanchez")
  
  tea <- tibble(
    record_id = paste0("TEA_", 1:n),
    first_name = sample(first_names, n, replace = TRUE),
    last_name = sample(last_names, n, replace = TRUE),
    dob = sample(seq(as.Date("1950-01-01"), as.Date("1985-12-31"), by = "day"), n),
    certification = sample(c("Science", "Math", "English", "Social Studies", "Special Ed"), n, replace = TRUE),
    school_district = sample(paste0("District_", 1:50), n, replace = TRUE),
    hire_date = sample(seq(as.Date("1990-01-01"), as.Date("2020-12-31"), by = "day"), n)
  )
  
  # Make the first num_matches TEA records true matches of TRS_1..TRS_num_matches.
  # The remaining TEA records are unrelated people (true non-matches).
  tea$first_name[1:num_matches] <- trs$first_name[1:num_matches]
  tea$last_name[1:num_matches] <- trs$last_name[1:num_matches]
  tea$dob[1:num_matches] <- trs$dob[1:num_matches]

  # Introduce data quality issues in the matched records only
  # About 20% of matched records have corruption or variation
  corruption_indices <- sample(1:num_matches, size = round(num_matches * corruption_rate), replace = FALSE)
  
  for (idx in corruption_indices) {
    flip <- sample(1:3, 1)
    
    if (flip == 1) {
      # Introduce name variation
      tea$first_name[idx] <- abbreviate(tea$first_name[idx], minlength = 3)
    } else if (flip == 2) {
      # Introduce small typo in last name
      last_chars <- nchar(tea$last_name[idx])
      if (last_chars > 1) {
        typo_pos <- sample(1:last_chars, 1)
        wrong_char <- sample(letters[!(letters %in% unlist(strsplit(tea$last_name[idx], "")))], 1)
        tea$last_name[idx] <- paste0(
          substr(tea$last_name[idx], 1, typo_pos - 1),
          wrong_char,
          substr(tea$last_name[idx], typo_pos + 1, last_chars)
        )
      }
    } else {
      # Shift DOB slightly (data entry error)
      tea$dob[idx] <- tea$dob[idx] + sample(c(-1, 1), 1)
    }
  }
  
  return(tea)
}

# Create a subset of KNOWN matches for validation
create_validation_set <- function(trs, tea, num_matches = 100) {
  
  # Take first 100 records from TRS
  trs_subset <- trs %>% slice(1:num_matches)
  
  # These are the "true" matches in TEA
  true_matches <- tea %>%
    slice(1:num_matches) %>%
    rename_with(~paste0("tea_", .), everything()) %>%
    rename(tea_record_id = tea_record_id)
  
  # Create ground truth
  validation <- tibble(
    trs_record_id = trs_subset$record_id,
    tea_record_id = true_matches$tea_record_id,
    is_match = TRUE
  )
  
  return(validation)
}

deterministic_linkage <- function(data_a, data_b, 
                                  id_col_a = "record_id", 
                                  id_col_b = "record_id") {
  
  log_info("Starting deterministic linkage...")
  
  matches <- tibble()
  remaining_a <- data_a
  remaining_b <- data_b
  
  # RULE 1: Exact match on last name + first name + DOB
  # (Highest confidence)
  log_info("Applying Rule 1: Last name + First name + DOB")
  
  rule1 <- remaining_a %>%
    inner_join(
      remaining_b,
      by = c("last_name_std" = "last_name_std",
             "first_name_std" = "first_name_std",
             "dob_std" = "dob_std"),
      suffix = c("_a", "_b")
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      rule_applied = "Rule_1_FullName_DOB",
      confidence = 0.99
    ) %>%
    select(!!sym(paste0(id_col_a, "_a")), 
           !!sym(paste0(id_col_b, "_b")), 
           rule_applied, confidence)
  
  matches <- bind_rows(matches, rule1)
  
  # Remove matched records
  remaining_a <- anti_join(remaining_a, rule1, by = setNames("record_id_a", id_col_a))
  remaining_b <- anti_join(remaining_b, rule1, by = setNames("record_id_b", id_col_b))
  
  log_info(paste("Rule 1 found", nrow(rule1), "matches"))
  
  # RULE 2: Last name + First initial + DOB
  # (For records where first name varies slightly)
  log_info("Applying Rule 2: Last name + First initial + DOB")
  
  rule2 <- remaining_a %>%
    inner_join(
      remaining_b,
      by = c("last_name_std" = "last_name_std",
             "first_initial" = "first_initial",
             "dob_std" = "dob_std"),
      suffix = c("_a", "_b")
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      rule_applied = "Rule_2_LastName_Initial_DOB",
      confidence = 0.95
    ) %>%
    select(record_id_a, record_id_b, rule_applied, confidence)

  matches <- bind_rows(matches, rule2)
  remaining_a <- anti_join(remaining_a, rule2, by = setNames("record_id_a", id_col_a))
  remaining_b <- anti_join(remaining_b, rule2, by = setNames("record_id_b", id_col_b))
  
  log_info(paste("Rule 2 found", nrow(rule2), "matches"))
  
  # RULE 3: Last name + First name + DOB within 1 day
  # (For data entry errors on DOB)
  log_info("Applying Rule 3: Last name + First name + DOB (±1 day)")
  
  rule3 <- remaining_a %>%
    cross_join(remaining_b, suffix = c("_a", "_b")) %>%
    filter(
      last_name_std_a == last_name_std_b,
      first_name_std_a == first_name_std_b,
      abs(as.numeric(difftime(dob_std_a, dob_std_b, units = "days"))) <= 1
    ) %>%
    select(record_id_a, record_id_b) %>%
    mutate(
      rule_applied = "Rule_3_DOBFlex",
      confidence = 0.90
    )

  if (nrow(rule3) > 0) {
    # Remove duplicates (keep first match only)
    rule3 <- rule3 %>% distinct(record_id_a, .keep_all = TRUE)
    matches <- bind_rows(matches, rule3)
    remaining_a <- anti_join(remaining_a, rule3, by = setNames("record_id_a", id_col_a))
    remaining_b <- anti_join(remaining_b, rule3, by = setNames("record_id_b", id_col_b))
  }
  
  log_info(paste("Rule 3 found", nrow(rule3), "matches"))
  
  result <- list(
    matches = matches,
    remaining_a = remaining_a,
    remaining_b = remaining_b,
    summary = tibble(
      Rule = c("Rule 1", "Rule 2", "Rule 3"),
      Matches = c(nrow(rule1), nrow(rule2), nrow(rule3))
    )
  )
  
  return(result)
}

# Calculate string similarity using Jaro-Winkler
calculate_string_similarity <- function(str1, str2, method = "jw") {
  
  if (is.na(str1) | is.na(str2)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  
  # Jaro-Winkler returns distance (0-1), we want similarity
  1 - stringdist(str1, str2, method = method)
}

# More efficient: Use vectorized stringdistmatrix
calculate_similarity_efficient <- function(data_a_field, data_b_field) {
  
  dist_matrix <- stringdistmatrix(
    data_a_field,
    data_b_field,
    method = "jw",
    useNames = "strings"
  )
  
  # Convert distance to similarity (1 - distance)
  similarity <- 1 - dist_matrix
  
  return(similarity)
}

# ============================================================================
# ASSESSMENT: PRECISION, RECALL, F1-SCORE
# ============================================================================

assess_linkage_quality <- function(all_matches, validation_set) {
  
  log_info("Assessing linkage quality against validation set...")
  
  our_matches <- all_matches %>%
    mutate(our_match = 1) %>%
    select(trs_record_id, tea_record_id, our_match)
  
  true_matches <- validation_set %>%
    rename(trs_record_id = trs_record_id, 
           tea_record_id = tea_record_id) %>%
    mutate(true_match = 1) %>%
    select(trs_record_id, tea_record_id, true_match)
  
  # Full outer join to get all possibilities
  assessment <- true_matches %>%
    full_join(our_matches, 
              by = c("trs_record_id", "tea_record_id")) %>%
    mutate(
      true_match = replace_na(true_match, 0),
      our_match = replace_na(our_match, 0)
    )
  
  tp <- sum(assessment$true_match == 1 & assessment$our_match == 1)
  fp <- sum(assessment$true_match == 0 & assessment$our_match == 1)
  fn <- sum(assessment$true_match == 1 & assessment$our_match == 0)
  tn <- sum(assessment$true_match == 0 & assessment$our_match == 0)
  
  precision <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else NA_real_
  recall <- if (tp + fn > 0) tp / (tp + fn) else NA_real_
  f1 <- if (!is.na(precision) & !is.na(recall) & precision + recall > 0) {
    2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall)
  } else {
    NA_real_
  }
  
  accuracy <- (tp + tn) / nrow(assessment)
  
  results <- list(
    metrics = tibble(
      Metric = c("Precision", "Recall", "F1-Score", "Accuracy"),
      Value = c(precision, recall, f1, accuracy),
      Interpretation = c(
        "Of matches we made, what % were correct?",
        "Of all true matches, what % did we find?",
        "Harmonic mean of precision and recall",
        "What % of all decisions were correct?"
      )
    ),
    confusion_matrix = tibble(
      Metric = c("True Positives", "False Positives", "False Negatives", "True Negatives"),
      Count = c(tp, fp, fn, tn)
    ),
    detailed = assessment
  )
  
  return(results)
}

sensitivity_analysis <- function(all_comparisons, validation_df = validation_set, include_deterministic = FALSE, det_matches = NULL) {
  
  log_info("Running sensitivity analysis on thresholds...")
  thresholds <- seq(0.70, 0.99, by = 0.05)
  results <- tibble()
  
  for (threshold in thresholds) {
    test_matches <- all_comparisons %>%
      filter(match_score >= threshold) %>%
      mutate(our_match = 1) %>%
      select(record_id_a, record_id_b, our_match)
    
    if (include_deterministic && !is.null(det_matches)) {
      test_matches <- bind_rows(
        det_matches %>% select(record_id_a, record_id_b) %>% mutate(our_match = 1),
        test_matches
      ) %>% distinct(record_id_a, record_id_b, .keep_all = TRUE)
    }
    
    # Full validation
    assessment <- validation_df %>%
      rename(record_id_a = trs_record_id, record_id_b = tea_record_id) %>%
      full_join(test_matches, by = c("record_id_a", "record_id_b")) %>%
      mutate(
        is_match = replace_na(is_match, 0),
        our_match = replace_na(our_match, 0)
      )
    
    tp <- sum(assessment$is_match == 1 & assessment$our_match == 1)
    fp <- sum(assessment$is_match == 0 & assessment$our_match == 1)
    fn <- sum(assessment$is_match == 1 & assessment$our_match == 0)
    
    precision <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else 0
    recall <- if (tp + fn > 0) tp / (tp + fn) else 0
    f1 <- if (precision + recall > 0) 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall) else 0
    
    results <- bind_rows(results, tibble(
      threshold = threshold,
      num_matches = nrow(test_matches),
      precision = precision,
      recall = recall,
      f1 = f1
    ))
  }
  return(results)
}

1. Read
Question: What does the Fellegi-Sunter model estimate that the workshop’s weighted score does not?
In comparison the the default linear scoring th Fellegi-Sunter model uses an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to the the observed agreement patterns without a training key. The Fellegi-Sunter model is able to get the posterior match probability for each candidate pairs using the priors and the field conditional probabilities of agreement.
Question: Why does the paper treat records with a unique ID differently from records without one?
When a unique identity field is available, a merge is quite easy as the linkages are clean and standardized. Without this identifier field, there is always a degree of uncertainty around if a given record is actually related to the records in the data set to which the merging is happening.

  fn_sim <- calculate_similarity_efficient(unm_a$first_name_std, unm_b$first_name_std)
  d_sim <- outer(
    as.numeric(unm_a$dob_std),
    as.numeric(unm_b$dob_std),
    function(x, y) {
      diff_days <- abs(x - y)
      ifelse(diff_days == 0, 1.0, ifelse(diff_days == 1, 0.95, 0.0))
    }
  )
  
  comps <- expand_grid(idx_a = 1:nrow(unm_a), idx_b = 1:nrow(unm_b)) %>%
    mutate(
      record_id_a = unm_a$record_id[idx_a],
      record_id_b = unm_b$record_id[idx_b],
      last_name_sim = ln_sim[cbind(idx_a, idx_b)],
      first_name_sim = fn_sim[cbind(idx_a, idx_b)],
      dob_sim = d_sim[cbind(idx_a, idx_b)],
      match_score = last_name_sim * weights[1] + first_name_sim * weights[2] + dob_sim * weights[3]
    ) %>%
    select(record_id_a, record_id_b, last_name_sim, first_name_sim, dob_sim, match_score)
  
  prob_links <- if (strict_gt) {
    comps %>% filter(match_score > threshold)
  } else {
    comps %>% filter(match_score >= threshold)
  }
  
  combined_matches <- bind_rows(
    det_r$matches %>% select(trs_record_id = record_id_a, tea_record_id = record_id_b) %>% mutate(source = "Deterministic"),
    prob_links %>% select(trs_record_id = record_id_a, tea_record_id = record_id_b) %>% mutate(source = "Probabilistic")
  )
  
  qa <- assess_linkage_quality(combined_matches, val_r)
  
  tibble(
    Corruption_Rate = rate,
    Rule_1 = det_r$summary$Matches[1],
    Rule_2 = det_r$summary$Matches[2],
    Rule_3 = det_r$summary$Matches[3],
    Probabilistic_Links = nrow(prob_links),
    Total_Links = nrow(combined_matches),
    Precision = qa$metrics$Value[qa$metrics$Metric == "Precision"],
    Recall = qa$metrics$Value[qa$metrics$Metric == "Recall"],
    F1_Score = qa$metrics$Value[qa$metrics$Metric == "F1-Score"]
  )
}

3a. Plot the Threshold Curve

evaluate_threshold_grid <- function(comparisons_df, det_matches_df, validation_df, scheme_label) {
  grid <- seq(0.70, 0.99, by = 0.01)
  map_dfr(grid, function(thresh) {
    prob_m <- comparisons_df %>%
      filter(match_score >= thresh) %>%
      select(trs_record_id = record_id_a, tea_record_id = record_id_b)
    
    comb_m <- bind_rows(
      det_matches_df %>% select(trs_record_id = record_id_a, tea_record_id = record_id_b),
      prob_m
    ) %>% distinct()
    
    assess <- validation_df %>%
      mutate(true_match = 1) %>%
      full_join(comb_m %>% mutate(our_match = 1), by = c("trs_record_id", "tea_record_id")) %>%
      mutate(true_match = replace_na(true_match, 0), our_match = replace_na(our_match, 0))
    
    tp <- sum(assess$true_match == 1 & assess$our_match == 1)
    fp <- sum(assess$true_match == 0 & assess$our_match == 1)
    fn <- sum(assess$true_match == 1 & assess$our_match == 0)
    
    prec <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else 0
    rec <- if (tp + fn > 0) tp / (tp + fn) else 0
    f1 <- if (prec + rec > 0) 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec) else 0
    
    tibble(
      Scheme = scheme_label,
      threshold = thresh,
      tp = tp, fp = fp, fn = fn,
      Precision = prec, Recall = rec, `F1-Score` = f1
    )
  })
}

3c. Review Band Analysis

analyze_review_band <- function(comparisons_df, lower_b, upper_b, upper_inclusive = TRUE, label = "") {
  band_df <- if (upper_inclusive) {
    comparisons_df %>% filter(match_score >= lower_b & match_score <= upper_b)
  } else {
    comparisons_df %>% filter(match_score >= lower_b & match_score < upper_b)
  }
  
  band_df <- band_df %>%
    left_join(validation_set, by = c("record_id_a" = "trs_record_id", "record_id_b" = "tea_record_id")) %>%
    mutate(is_match = replace_na(is_match, FALSE))
  
  n_total <- nrow(band_df)
  n_true <- sum(band_df$is_match)
  share_correct <- if (n_total > 0) n_true / n_total else NA_real_
  
  tibble(
    Review_Band_Config = label,
    Band_Range = paste0("[", lower_b, ", ", upper_b, ifelse(upper_inclusive, "]", ")")),
    Pairs_In_Band = n_total,
    True_Matches = n_true,
    False_Positives = n_total - n_true,
    Share_Correct = share_correct
  )
}

Under the default (\(\tau > 0.95\), default weights): False positives contribute +0 records in the upward direction (\(\text{FP} = 0\)), while false negatives remove -3 records in the downward direction (\(\text{FN} = 3\)). The estimated overlap is \(\hat{N} = 97\) versus the true count of \(100\), resulting in a net downward bias (undercount) of \(-3\) people (\(-3.0\%\)). At the 0.40 corruption rate, this downward bias more than doubles to \(-7\) people (\(-7.0\%\), \(\hat{N} = 93\)). Crucially, this undercount is not uniform across demographic groups: because 5-letter surnames (Smith, Brown, Jones, Davis, Lopez) score \(0.9467\) when corrupted by a 1-character typo while 6-to-9 letter surnames score \(\ge 0.9556\), individuals with short surnames suffer \(100\%\) of the false negatives.
Under a loose threshold (\(\tau = 0.80\), default weights): False negatives contribute 0 downward error (\(\text{FN} = 0\)), while false positives add +3 erroneous links in the upward direction (\(\text{FP} = 3\)), creating a net upward bias (overcount) of \(+3\) people (\(+3.0\%\), \(\hat{N} = 103\)).

5. Report: Linking TRS and TEA Administrative Records

i. Research Question the Linked File Answers
In the area of public education researchers and analyst frequently need to connect records. Hence the research question would be, how many active TEA-certified teachers are enrolled in the TRS system, and how do retention and reirement patterns vary across subject and district?


ii. Chosen Linkage Method, Threshold, and Prioritized Metric
Method: two-stage hybrid linkage pipeline followingFoster et al. (2020, chap. 3) and Enamorado, Fifield, and Imai (2019). Threshold: normalized Fellegi-Sunter log-likelihood ratio 0.1761 / 0.1818 / 0.6421 Prioritized metric: Precision

iv. Threshold Calibration Curve
This shows how Precision, Recall, and F1-Score move from \(\tau = 0.70\) to \(\tau = 0.99\). At \(\tau = 0.70\), default weights have 607 false positives because 601 unrelated pairs share identical common first and last names.


v. Limits of the Linked File and Sensitivity to the Answer Key
The linked file is not reality, it is guess that two records contain the same person.

Whose records are more likely to be missed or linked wrongly: Under string-similarity scoring, single-character typos penalize short surnames much more heavily than 9-letter surnames, causing short-surname educators to be disproportionately dropped at high thresholds. Conversely, educators from demographic groups with high surname concentration face a much higher baseline collision rate, increasing false-positive risks when birthdates are missing or noisy. Furthermore, in real TEA/TRS files, women and younger educators who change surnames upon marriage or divorce will fail both surname blocking and surname similarity rules if historical name tables are unavailable.
What the linked file cannot tell you: The linked file cannot distinguish whether an unlinked TRS member is genuinely absent from TEA or is a certified teacher whose record failed linkage due to a marital name change or multi-field corruption.
What would change if the answer key were wrong or unavailable: In our simulation, we know with \(100\%\) confidence that TRS_1..TRS_100 correspond to TEA_1..TEA_100. In real administrative merges, no ground-truth answer key exists, or a “gold standard” training sample is constructed from clerical review of easy cases. If our answer key omitted hard-to-link cases (such as marital surname changes or multi-field errors), our evaluation would severely overstate recall and understate optimal review-band width. For our conclusions to hold without an answer key, the conditional independence assumption across fields given match status and the missing-at-random / homogeneous corruption assumption across school districts and demographic groups must hold (Enamorado, Fifield, and Imai 2019, 356–359)—assumptions that should be audited via clerical sampling and post-linkage uncertainty weighting.

title: Assignment 8
text:
6. Data Note & Academic Integrity Statement

Data Note (Section 6b)

Source: Simulated administrative datasets representing the Teacher Retirement System of Texas (TRS, \(N = 500\)) and the Texas Education Agency (TEA, \(N = 500\)), generated in R using set.seed(42) across three corruption rates (0.10, 0.20 baseline, and 0.40) applied to num_matches = 100 true overlapping records (TRS_1..TRS_100 paired with TEA_1..TEA_100).
Method:

Preprocessing: Standardized first and last names to lowercase ASCII letters (standardize_names()), extracted first initial (substr(first_name_std, 1, 1)), and standardized dates of birth to Date format.
Deterministic Rules: Sequential exact matching on (Rule 1) last_name_std + first_name_std + dob_std, (Rule 2) last_name_std + first_initial + dob_std, and (Rule 3) last_name_std + first_name_std with |dob_a - dob_b| <= 1 day, removing matched records after each rule via anti_join().
Blocking: Blocked residual unmatched records on the first letter of standardized surname (substr(last_name_std_a, 1, 1) == substr(last_name_std_b, 1, 1)), reducing baseline candidate pairs from \(407 \times 407 = 165,649\) to \(19,030\) (\(-88.51\%\)).
Weights & Scoring: Compared baseline intuition weights (0.40 / 0.30 / 0.30) against empirical Fellegi-Sunter \(\log(m/u)\) weights (0.1754 / 0.1803 / 0.6443) and unsupervised EM weights (0.1761 / 0.1818 / 0.6421) using Jaro string similarity (stringdist(..., method = "jw")) and step-function DOB similarity (\(1.0\) exact, \(0.95\) for \(\pm 1\) day, \(0.0\) otherwise).
Threshold: Calibrated automatic link threshold at \(\tau = 0.90\) under default weights and \(\tau = 0.95\) under \(\log(m/u)\) weights, with a manual review band of \([0.85, 0.95]\).

Selection (What the Simulation and Answer Key Leave Out): The simulation draws uniformly from 12 first names and 12 surnames (18 first names and 16 surnames in TEA) with uniform birthdates between 1950-01-01 and 1985-12-31, and corrupts at most one field per true match (either a 3-letter first-name abbreviation, a 1-character surname typo, or a \(\pm 1\) day DOB shift) while leaving all 400 true non-matches uncorrupted. It leaves out multi-field corruptions, marital or hyphenated surname changes, middle names/suffixes, nicknames that change the first initial (e.g., Robert -> Bob, William -> Bill), twin birthdates, missing/NULL fields, and longitudinal duplicate records within the same agency.
Known Gaps & Privacy Practice: Single-pass blocking on the first letter of last_name_std drops true matches whenever a typo occurs in the first character of a surname (3 unreachable matches at corruption_rate = 0.40). In accordance with Section 6c privacy standards, raw generated names and birthdates are suppressed from exported tables, which display only de-identified record IDs (TRS_*, TEA_*), similarity scores, and institutional attributes.
